introduction-the-millisecond-imperative.core: In-memory caches return data in sub-millisecond time versus several milliseconds or more for databases, absorbing repeated reads, cutting database load and cost, and storing ephemeral data (sessions, rate limits, leaderboards). ElastiCache runs managed Redis OSS, Valkey and Memcached.

first_principles.problem: A product page makes 40 database queries and the database melts during a sale.
derivation: **Cache-aside**: read cache, on miss read DB and populate.

analogy.title: A chef's mise en place
analogy.story: Pre-chopped ingredients within reach, instead of going to the pantry for every dish.
analogy.breaks: Prepped ingredients spoil visibly; stale cache data looks perfectly fine.

check.q: What happens on a cache miss in cache-aside?
check.a: The app reads from the database, then writes the value into the cache for next time.

memcached-vs-redis-the-first-choice.core: Memcached is a simple, multithreaded key-value cache with no persistence, replication or rich types, which makes it good for plain object caching that scales vertically. Redis/Valkey adds data structures (hashes, sorted sets, streams), replication, Multi-AZ failover, persistence options, pub/sub, Lua and cluster mode. It's the default for most use cases.

first_principles.problem: A team picks Memcached and later needs leaderboards and failover.
truths: Rich structures enable new use cases.
derivation: Pick Memcached only for **pure, disposable caching**.

analogy.title: A notepad versus a whiteboard with filing trays
analogy.story: The notepad is quick; the whiteboard organises, sorts and has a backup photo.
analogy.breaks: Notepads last; Memcached loses everything on node failure.

check.q: Which engine supports replication and automatic failover?

redis-cluster-mode-disabled-vs-enabled.core: Cluster mode disabled has one shard (a primary plus up to 5 replicas): simple, with all keys on one node, and scales reads only. Cluster mode enabled splits the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots across up to 500 shards, scaling writes and memory horizontally, but multi-key operations must stay in one slot (use hash tags).

first_principles.problem: A single Redis primary runs out of memory and write capacity.
truths: One node has finite memory and CPU.
derivation: **Disabled** for small datasets and read scaling.
**Enabled** for large datasets and write scaling.
Use **{hash tags}** to co-locate related keys.

analogy.title: One big filing cabinet versus a room of cabinets
analogy.story: With many cabinets you store more and more people can file at once, but related files must share a cabinet.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets can be searched together by hand; cross-slot commands fail outright.

code.text:
SET {user:42}:profile ...
SET {user:42}:cart ...
# both hash on 'user:42' → same slot → MULTI/EXEC works

check.q: How many hash slots does Redis Cluster use?

global-datastore-going-multi-region.core: Global Datastore replicates a Redis/Valkey cluster from a primary region to up to two secondary regions with typically sub-second lag. Secondaries serve local low-latency reads and can be promoted during a regional outage. Writes go to the primary region only.

first_principles.problem: Users in Asia see 200 ms cache reads from a US cluster, and a US outage means a cold cache.
derivation: Create **Global Datastore** from a primary cluster.

analogy.title: A franchise menu printed centrally and sent to branches abroad
analogy.story: Branches read their local copy; changes only come from head office.
analogy.breaks: Menus change rarely; cache data changes constantly, so lag matters.

example.title: Global session store
flow: Writes forwarded by app to us-east-1

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fast reads globally, warm DR cache.

check.q: Can secondary regions in Global Datastore accept writes?
check.a: No; writes go to the primary region, while secondaries serve reads until promoted.

cache-eviction-policies-and-ttl-strategy.core: When memory fills, Redis evicts keys per maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru/lfu (any key), volatile-lru/lfu/ttl (only keys with TTLs) or noeviction (writes fail). TTLs bound staleness and memory. Add jitter to TTLs to avoid synchronised expiry and stampedes.

first_principles.problem: Memory fills and writes start failing with OOM errors, or thousands of keys expire at once and hammer the database.
truths: Some keys are hotter than others.
derivation: Choose **volatile-*** when mixing persistent and cache keys.

analogy.title: Clearing out a fridge
analogy.story: When full, toss the food you use least; label everything with a use-by date, staggered so you don't restock everything on one day.
analogy.breaks: Fridges hold food you'll eventually need; cache entries can always be recomputed.

code.text:
import random
ttl = 3600 + random.randint(0, 300)
r.setex(key, ttl, value)

check.q: What happens with maxmemory-policy noeviction when memory is full?
check.a: Write commands that need memory return errors instead of evicting keys.

cache-invalidation-patterns.core: Keeping cache and database consistent uses patterns: TTL-based expiry (eventual), delete-on-write (invalidate after updating the DB), write-through (update cache with DB), event-driven invalidation from change streams (CDC), and versioned keys. Guard against stampedes with locks or request coalescing and stale-while-revalidate.

first_principles.problem: Users see stale prices after updates, and an expired hot key triggers 5,000 simultaneous DB queries.
truths: Two stores can't be updated atomically.
Deleting is safer than updating the cache.

analogy.title: Updating a shop's price tags
analogy.story: Change the master price list first, then remove old tags; staff fetch new tags when they notice one missing.
analogy.breaks: Shop staff coordinate naturally; concurrent requests can race, re-caching old values.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One DB query per expiry, not thousands.

check.q: Why delete the cache key instead of updating it after a DB write?
check.a: Deleting avoids races where an older value overwrites a newer one; the next read repopulates from the DB.
